title: Restaurant and Franchise Training Video Translation
excerpt: The kitchen and the dining room often do not speak the same language, and the training is usually written for the dining room.

children.text: ![Professional kitchen with chefs at work
](https://octavia.lunartech.ai)
Two Workforces in One Building
Restaurants have a structural language pattern that most other businesses do not: the front of house and the back of house frequently have different linguistic profiles.

Service staff are customer-facing and generally hired for local-language fluency. Kitchen staff are not customer-facing, and in most urban markets the kitchen workforce is substantially migrant, with a first language other than the language of the menu, the manager, or the training material.

This produces a predictable failure. Training is written and delivered in the operating language, service staff follow it comfortably, and the kitchen — where food safety, allergen control, equipment hazards, and product consistency all live — follows it partially, supplemented by demonstration and by whichever colleague can interpret.
The consequences are concrete. Food safety failures, allergen incidents, inconsistent product, equipment injuries, and the operational overhead of a chef who spends their shift re-explaining things.
Restaurants are also a sector where the case for localization is easy to quantify, because food safety audits, complaint rates, wastage, and consistency scores are already measured.
Content That Matters Most

Food safety and hygiene. Temperature control, cross-contamination, cleaning and sanitising procedures, personal hygiene, date labelling, and cooling and reheating procedure. Legally mandated in most jurisdictions, audited, and where errors cause illness.
Allergen management. In many markets a specific legal obligation with severe consequences for failure. This is the single highest-stakes content in a restaurant.
Recipe and specification adherence. How each dish is built, portioned, and presented. The direct driver of consistency and of food cost.
Equipment operation and safety. Fryers, slicers, ovens, mixers, and cleaning chemicals. The main injury sources in commercial kitchens.
Opening, closing, and changeover procedures. Highly proceduralised, repeated daily, and a common source of drift.
Service standards and customer interaction. Front of house, and the content most needing adaptation rather than translation.
Licensing and compliance. Age-restricted sales, responsible service of alcohol, and local regulatory requirements.
The rational priority is allergens and food safety first, then recipe specification, then equipment. Those three cover legal exposure, product quality, and injury risk respectively.
Allergens Deserve Disclosure-Level Treatment
Allergen content should be handled with the rigour applied to regulated disclosures rather than as ordinary training material.

The reasons are specific. Allergen requirements are legally defined, the allergen list itself is a legal schedule that varies by jurisdiction, the consequences of error include death, and the person who needs to understand the information is frequently the person least well served by the operating-language training.
Practical controls:

Use the local regulator's official allergen terminology. Most jurisdictions publish the regulated allergen list with official names in the local language. Use those exact terms rather than generated translations. A generated synonym for a regulated allergen name is both less accurate and indefensible in an investigation.

Check the allergen schedule per market. The regulated list differs between jurisdictions. Translating the source market's list produces a compliant-looking video that omits an allergen the local regulator requires.

Never soften the procedure. Allergen instruction is absolute — separate equipment, dedicated utensils, verify before serving. Fluent translation drifts toward hedging, which in this context is dangerous.

Cover the communication chain explicitly. The critical failure is usually not knowledge but transmission: a customer tells a server, the server tells the kitchen, the kitchen acts. Every link needs to work across the language boundary, and training should address that boundary directly rather than pretending it does not exist.
Verify comprehension, not attendance. Where assessment determines whether someone may handle allergen orders, that assessment must be in a language they genuinely understand.
![Chef plating a dish in a restaurant kitchen
](https://octavia.lunartech.ai)
Terminology and the Kitchen Lexicon

Kitchen vocabulary is a genuine mix: culinary terms that are French or Italian regardless of the operating language, brand-specific product and process names, equipment names, and local regulatory vocabulary.
Terms requiring locked renderings:
The regulated allergen list, in the regulator's official local terminology.
Temperature, time, and measurement vocabulary with correct local unit conventions.
Equipment names as they appear on the machines and in the kitchen.
Brand-specific recipe, product, and process names, which are usually retained rather than translated.
Culinary technique terms, many of which are borrowed and should stay borrowed.
Cleaning chemical names and their safety instructions, matched to the container labels.
Date labelling and stock rotation vocabulary.
Role titles as used in the operation.

The chemical labelling point is worth emphasising. Cleaning and sanitising products carry hazard labelling in the local language, and training that uses different vocabulary from the container leaves the worker unable to match instruction to product — which is exactly the situation that produces chemical injuries and food contamination.

Measurement conventions also need explicit handling. Temperature scales, weight units, and volume units differ by market, and a recipe specification with a mechanically converted temperature is a food safety issue rather than a rounding matter.
Franchise Networks
Most large restaurant brands operate substantially through franchisees, which reproduces the assurance gap seen across other distributed sectors.
The franchisor owns the brand, the specification, and the compliance risk. The franchisee employs the staff and controls training time, which is a direct labour cost to them.
What works:
Lead with compliance and consistency, which franchisees genuinely care about. A failed food safety inspection or an allergen incident hurts the franchisee immediately.

Provide the languages their kitchens actually speak. A franchisee whose kitchen team speaks Spanish or Bengali will use material in those languages and will not use English-only material, regardless of what the agreement says.
Keep modules short. Training time is money to a franchisee in a way it is not in a corporate store.
Make completion tracking useful to them, showing which of their staff are certified for allergen handling rather than merely reporting compliance upward.
Handle menu changes centrally. Franchisees will not localize new product training themselves, so a menu change without localized training means the new item is made inconsistently across the network.
Menu Change Cycles
Restaurant content has a volatility pattern that shapes the workflow.
Food safety, equipment, and hygiene content is stable for years. Recipe and product content changes with every menu cycle, promotion, and seasonal item — which in some brands means monthly.
Practices that keep this manageable:
Segment by volatility. Build stable content as a permanent library and product content as short discrete modules that can be replaced without touching anything else.

Template the recurring structure. New product training follows the same shape every time: what it is, ingredients and allergens, build specification, presentation, holding times. Templating means each new item localizes as a small delta rather than a fresh production.
Batch at the menu cycle boundary. All languages for a menu change processed together, which is exactly the workload profile batch processing suits.
Set expiry on promotional content, so discontinued items do not linger in the library.
Keep allergen data separate and versioned, since it changes independently of the recipe when a supplier changes.
![Restaurant team briefing before service
](https://octavia.lunartech.ai)
Delivery in an Operating Kitchen
Phones, in breaks, in noisy environments. Localized audio plus high-contrast captions, both.
Short modules. Two to four minutes. Kitchen staff do not have thirty-minute training slots.
Findable at the point of need. A cook who needs to check a specification mid-shift needs the relevant thirty seconds, not a course.

Visual and demonstrative. Cooking is a physical skill, and demonstration carries more than narration. This works in localization's favour, since the visual layer is language-independent and only the narration needs replacing.
Offline capability. Kitchen connectivity is frequently poor.
Pre-shift and pre-arrival delivery. New starter content sent before the first shift removes training from the operating hours.
Measuring It
Restaurants measure a lot already, and the effects surface quickly.

Worth segmenting by language of training delivery: food safety audit and inspection scores; allergen incident and near-miss reports; customer complaint rates related to product accuracy; food cost and wastage, which respond directly to specification adherence; equipment injury rates; consistency and mystery-diner scores; and thirty-day attrition, which in hospitality is high and substantially driven by new starters feeling lost.

Allergen near-miss reporting is a particularly useful early indicator, and rates often rise initially after localized training — not because incidents increased but because staff who now understand the procedure start reporting them.
A Working Checklist
Localize allergen and food safety content first, using the local regulator's official terminology.
Verify the regulated allergen list per market rather than translating the source market's list.
Address the front-of-house to kitchen communication chain explicitly.
Match cleaning chemical vocabulary to the container labelling.
Handle temperature, weight, and volume conventions per market, not by mechanical conversion.
Segment stable content from volatile product content and template the latter.
Batch all languages at the menu cycle boundary.
Build two-to-four-minute modules, offline-capable, with audio and captions.
Organise content for mid-shift lookup, not only sequential completion.
Provide franchisees with material in the languages their kitchens actually speak.
Building the Certification Layer
Food safety and allergen competence is frequently tied to formal certification, and localizing the training without localizing the assessment leaves the programme half-built.
Practical requirements:

Assess in the language of instruction. A cook trained in Bengali and assessed in English is being tested partly on English comprehension rather than on food safety competence, which invalidates the assessment for its actual purpose.

Revalidate question difficulty per language. Distractors in multiple-choice items are carefully constructed to be plausibly wrong, and translation can render them obviously wrong or accidentally correct. Time-limited assessments also become harder in languages with longer text.

Record language of delivery on the certificate. In an inspection or an incident investigation, the relevant question is whether that individual received comprehensible instruction, and the training record is the evidence.
Set refresher cycles per person, not per site. High turnover means a site-level annual cycle leaves individuals uncovered for months.
Gate allergen handling on verified competence. Where only certified staff may take allergen orders, the system should enforce it rather than relying on a rota someone maintains manually.

Keep the certification list visible to the manager on shift. A duty manager needs to know at a glance who on the floor tonight is certified for allergen handling, and that information being buried in a head-office system defeats its purpose.
Frequently Asked Questions
Why does allergen content need special handling?

Because the allergen list is a legal schedule that varies by jurisdiction, the terminology is officially defined, and the consequences of error include death. Use the local regulator's published allergen names rather than generated translations, verify the regulated list for each market rather than translating the source market's version, and never allow absolute procedural language to soften in translation.
Our kitchen and service staff speak different languages. What do we localize?

Both, but prioritise the kitchen, because that is where food safety, allergen control, equipment hazards, and product consistency live, and it is usually the workforce least well served by operating-language training. Also address the communication chain between them explicitly — most allergen failures are transmission failures at that boundary rather than knowledge failures.
How do we keep up with menu changes across many languages?

Segment stable content from volatile product content, template the recurring new-product structure so each item localizes as a small delta, and batch all languages together at the menu cycle boundary. Set expiry dates on promotional content so discontinued items do not linger, and version allergen data separately since it changes when suppliers change.
How do we get franchisees to use the training?

Lead with compliance and consistency, which affect them directly through inspections and incidents, keep modules short since training time is a direct labour cost to them, provide the languages their kitchens actually speak, and make completion tracking useful to them — showing which staff are certified for allergen handling rather than only reporting upward.
What should we measure?

Food safety audit scores, allergen near-misses, complaint rates for product accuracy, wastage and food cost, equipment injuries, consistency scores, and thirty-day attrition, all segmented by the language training was delivered in. Expect allergen near-miss reporting to rise at first — that usually indicates staff now understand the procedure well enough to recognise and report a problem.

title: Retail Frontline Training Video Translation
excerpt: Retail trains more people per year than almost any industry, and reaches fewer of them than it thinks.

children.text: ![Retail store interior with product displays
](https://octavia.lunartech.ai)
The Deskless Majority
Retail employs an enormous, distributed, multilingual workforce that does not sit at desks, does not have corporate email in many cases, and turns over faster than almost any other sector.

That combination breaks most of the assumptions corporate learning teams build around. Content designed for someone with a laptop, a scheduled training slot, and a stable email address reaches a fraction of a retail workforce. Content designed for a phone, a fifteen-minute break, and a worker who started nine days ago reaches most of it.

Language sits on top of that. In many urban markets, a store team may include several first languages, and the staff most likely to be serving customers in a given community may be the ones least well served by head-office training material.

The commercial case is unusually direct in retail, because the link between staff knowledge and revenue is short. A colleague who understands the product recommends it. A colleague who understands the returns policy resolves a complaint instead of escalating it. A colleague who understands the safety procedure does not cause an incident that closes an aisle.
What Retail Actually Trains On
The content divides into categories with quite different localization economics.

Onboarding and induction. Store layout, systems access, health and safety, security procedure, customer service standards, and company basics. Delivered constantly, largely stable, and the highest-volume content in most retailers.
Product knowledge. Changes seasonally or faster. High value where products are complex or high-margin, low value where they are self-explanatory. The volatile category.
Systems and process. Point of sale, stock systems, click-and-collect, returns, age verification, and payment procedures. Stable, procedural, and where errors have direct commercial cost.
Compliance. Age-restricted sales, food safety and allergens, data protection, anti-money-laundering where relevant, and health and safety. Often legally mandated, often audited.
Loss prevention and security. Theft procedure, personal safety, conflict de-escalation, and incident reporting.
Customer service and selling. Behavioural rather than procedural, and the hardest to localize well because register and cultural norms matter.

The rational sequence is to localize onboarding, compliance, and systems first — high volume, stable, and consequential — and to treat volatile product knowledge as a subtitle-only tier unless the product line genuinely warrants more.
Seasonal Hiring Waves
Most retailers hire in waves, and the peak wave is the moment when training capacity is most stretched and the workforce is least experienced.

The operational pattern is familiar: hire several thousand people over six weeks, induct them under time pressure, and rely on experienced colleagues to fill the gaps — except that during peak, experienced colleagues are the busiest and least available.

Localized content changes this in a specific way. Content a new starter can watch on their own phone, in their own language, before their first shift or during a break, removes the dependency on someone being free to explain. That is worth more during peak than at any other time.
Practical approaches:
Build a short-tenure variant. A seasonal hire working eight weeks does not need the full curriculum. They need safety, systems, the specific tasks they will do, and the customer basics.
Deliver before the first shift. Pre-arrival content converts training time from a floor cost into the worker's own time, and gives them room to watch at their own pace.
Design for repeated reference. Seasonal staff will forget things. Short, findable modules they can rewatch beat a single long induction.
Re-induct returners quickly. Many seasonal staff return year over year and need a refresher rather than the full programme.
![Retail staff member assisting a customer
](https://octavia.lunartech.ai)
Franchise and Concession Networks
Many retailers operate partly or wholly through franchisees, and this reproduces the assurance problem seen in construction subcontracting and warehouse agency labour.
The franchisor sets standards and carries brand risk. The franchisee employs the staff. Training obligations flow through an agreement rather than an employment relationship, and compliance varies.
What works:
Make the content genuinely useful, not just mandated. Franchisees adopt training that visibly improves their numbers and resist training that feels like head-office overhead.
Provide it in the languages their staff actually speak. A franchisee with a predominantly Spanish-speaking team will use Spanish material and will quietly skip English-only material.
Track completion centrally where the agreement permits, and make the reporting useful to the franchisee rather than purely extractive.
Cover compliance content especially thoroughly. Age-restricted sales and food safety failures at a franchise damage the brand regardless of who employed the person who made the error.
Keep it short. Franchisee labour budgets are tight and training time is a direct cost to them in a way it is not to a corporate store.
Terminology and Brand Voice
Retail terminology is a mix of universal, brand-specific, and market-specific vocabulary.
Terms requiring locked renderings:
System names and screen labels, matched exactly to the point-of-sale and stock system as localized in that market.
Product category and range names as used in that market, which frequently differ from the source market.
Policy names — returns, exchanges, guarantees, loyalty programmes — matched to what appears on signage and receipts.
Role titles as used locally.
Compliance vocabulary, matched to the local regulator's terminology for age restrictions, allergens, and consumer rights.
Brand terms and taglines, which may be translated, adapted, or retained depending on the market strategy.

The alignment requirement is the same as elsewhere: if the training says one thing and the till screen says another, the colleague cannot connect them. Source system terminology from whoever localized the system interface, not independently.

Brand voice deserves separate thought. Retail training frequently carries a deliberately upbeat corporate register that translates badly. Direct translation of enthusiastic English marketing language into some target languages produces something that reads as insincere or childish. Adaptation rather than translation is usually right for the customer-service and brand-values content, even where straight translation is correct for procedure.
Delivery to a Deskless Workforce
Personal phones are the primary device. Assume modest hardware and metered data.
In-store connectivity is variable. Offline capability matters, particularly in large stores and basements.
Time comes in fragments. Modules of three to five minutes fit a break; thirty-minute courses do not.
Environments are noisy. Provide localized audio and captions both, not one or the other.
Email is unreliable as a channel. Many frontline staff do not check corporate email. Distribution via the workforce app, messaging, or a QR code in the break room reaches more people.
Make it findable later. A colleague facing an unusual return at the till needs to find the relevant ninety seconds, not rewatch an induction.

That last point is a genuine design difference between retail and most corporate training. The content is reference material as much as it is instruction, and organising it for lookup rather than for sequential completion changes how much value it delivers.
![Team meeting in a store back office
](https://octavia.lunartech.ai)
Measuring the Return
Retail is well instrumented and the effects show up quickly.

Metrics worth segmenting by language of training delivery: compliance audit pass rates, particularly age-restricted sales test purchases; till and transaction error rates; returns and complaint escalation rates; safety incident rates; attachment and upsell rates where product knowledge is the driver; time-to-competence for new starters; and early attrition in the first thirty days.

Early attrition is again the metric that often makes the case internally. Retail attrition in the first month is expensive and substantially driven by new starters feeling lost. Colleagues who received training they could actually follow are measurably more likely to still be there in week five.
Mystery shopping and audit programmes also give a direct read on whether knowledge landed, and segmenting those results by store language profile is straightforward for most retailers.
A Working Checklist
Localize onboarding, compliance, and systems content first; treat volatile product knowledge as a subtitle tier.
Build a short-tenure variant for seasonal hires rather than the full curriculum.
Deliver induction content before the first shift where possible.
Organise content for lookup and rewatching, not only sequential completion.
Source system and policy terminology from the localized interface and signage, not independently.
Adapt rather than translate brand-voice and customer-service content.
Distribute through the workforce app or messaging rather than corporate email.
Build three-to-five-minute modules, offline-capable, with audio and captions.
Provide franchisees with content in the languages their staff speak.
Segment audit, error, incident, and thirty-day attrition data by training language.
Governing Content Across Markets
Retail groups operating in several countries face a coordination problem that single-market retailers do not.

Central versus local content ownership. Compliance and systems content is usually best owned centrally, since the systems are shared. Customer service and brand behaviour content frequently needs local ownership, because service norms genuinely differ between markets.

Terminology must be sourced locally. System screen labels, policy names, and product category names differ per market because the localized systems differ. A central glossary that ignores this produces training that contradicts the till.

Compliance content cannot be shared blindly. Age restrictions, consumer rights, allergen rules, and data protection obligations vary by jurisdiction. Translating the source market's compliance module produces something that looks correct and is legally wrong.

Decide who can adapt. Local teams will want to adjust content, which is often legitimate. What matters is that adaptation is visible and routed through approval rather than happening silently in a local file share.
Version centrally, publish locally. The source content is versioned once; each market's localized version derives from it and flags stale automatically when the source changes.

Watch for shadow content. When local teams produce their own unofficial training material, it is a signal that the central library is not usable for them — usually because of language, length, or relevance rather than quality.
Groups that get this balance right find the central library carries most of the volume while local teams own the small proportion that genuinely needs to differ.
Frequently Asked Questions
Is localizing training worth it for seasonal staff who work eight weeks?

Usually yes, because seasonal staff have no accumulated experience and arrive when experienced colleagues are least available to help. A short-tenure module variant keeps the cost proportionate, and the return shows up in first-month attrition and transaction error rates, both of which are expensive in a large seasonal ramp.
How do we get franchisees to actually use localized training?

Make it visibly useful to their numbers rather than framing it as a compliance obligation, keep modules short since training time is a direct cost to them, and provide it in the languages their staff actually speak. Franchisees quietly skip English-only material for predominantly non-English teams, and no amount of mandating changes that.
Should brand and customer-service content be translated or adapted?

Adapted. Retail training often carries a deliberately upbeat corporate register that translates badly — enthusiastic English marketing language rendered literally can read as insincere or childish in several target languages. Procedure and compliance content can be translated straightforwardly; brand voice and service behaviour benefit from adaptation.
Where should retail terminology come from?

From the localized system interface, signage, and receipts in that market. System screen labels, policy names, and product category names must match what the colleague actually sees at the till and on the shop floor. Source it from whoever localized the point-of-sale and stock systems rather than building a training glossary independently.
How should content reach staff who do not use corporate email?

Through the workforce app, messaging platforms, or a QR code posted in the break room. A large share of frontline retail staff do not check corporate email, and distribution assumptions built around desk-based employees are the most common reason training reaches a fraction of the intended audience.
Should we localize training for a market where staff speak the operating language?

Check the assumption before accepting it. Store teams in many urban markets include colleagues whose everyday fluency is strong but whose comprehension of dense procedural or compliance content is not, and those are frequently the colleagues serving the local community. Assessment pass rates segmented by first language usually answer this question quickly and definitively.
How do we stop localized training going stale?

Version the source content so every language flags stale automatically when it changes, batch corrections rather than fixing individually, and put expiry dates on anything covering promotions, pricing, or seasonal ranges. Retail content changes faster than most sectors, and a library without automatic staleness flagging drifts within a single trading year.

title: Logistics and Warehouse Training Video Translation
excerpt: A warehouse that hires four hundred agency workers for peak season has four hundred inductions to deliver in six weeks.

children.text: ![Warehouse interior with racking and forklift
](https://octavia.lunartech.ai)
Turnover Is the Defining Constraint

Warehousing and logistics has a workforce profile unlike most industries: high turnover, heavy use of agency and temporary labour, dramatic seasonal surges, and a workforce that in most developed markets is substantially migrant and multilingual.

The operational consequence is that onboarding is not an occasional event. A large distribution centre may induct hundreds of people in a peak-season ramp, many of whom will work for a few weeks, and many of whom follow the induction language imperfectly.

This changes what good training looks like. In a stable workforce, you can invest heavily in a small number of people and rely on accumulated experience. In a high-turnover environment, the training material itself has to carry the load, because there is no accumulated experience to fall back on and no time for informal knowledge transfer.

Localization matters more here than the hazard profile alone would suggest, because the alternative — learning by watching experienced colleagues — is unavailable when half the shift started last week.
The Hazard Profile
Warehouse hazards are less dramatic than construction but more frequent, and several of them are precisely the kind that instruction prevents.
Powered industrial trucks. Forklifts, reach trucks, order pickers, and pallet trucks account for a substantial share of serious warehouse injuries, most involving pedestrians rather than operators.
Racking and storage. Collapse, falling stock, and incorrect loading.
Manual handling. The largest single source of lost-time injury in the sector, and one where technique instruction genuinely changes outcomes.
Vehicle and yard operations. Loading bay incidents, reversing, trailer movement, and the interface between yard traffic and pedestrians.
Working at height. Order picking, racking access, and mezzanine work.
Slips, trips, and housekeeping. Unglamorous and consistently the highest-frequency incident category.
Automation interfaces. Increasingly, conveyor systems, sorters, and robotics with specific isolation and access procedures.
Most of these are addressed by short, task-specific instruction that recurs identically across sites — which is exactly the content profile that localizes efficiently at scale.
Content Worth Localizing First
Site induction. Layout, pedestrian routes, traffic separation, emergency arrangements, muster points, reporting. Delivered to everyone, including agency staff on day one.
Pedestrian and vehicle segregation. The single highest-consequence topic in the sector.
Manual handling technique. Highest-frequency injury category, and instruction demonstrably reduces it.
Equipment-specific operation and pre-use checks for each truck type in use.
Racking safety and damage reporting. Including how to report damage, which is frequently not done because workers do not know the process.
Emergency procedure. Evacuation, spillage, fire, first aid, and how to raise an alarm.
Peak-season temporary worker onboarding, condensed into what a short-tenure worker genuinely needs.

The last one deserves separate design. A worker on a six-week contract does not need the full induction curriculum; they need the subset that keeps them safe and productive in their actual role. Building a short-tenure variant rather than pushing everyone through the full programme improves both completion and retention of what matters.
![Forklift operating in a distribution centre
](https://octavia.lunartech.ai)
Agency Labour and the Verification Gap
Much of the workforce arrives through agencies, which creates the same assurance problem construction has with subcontractors.

The agency is contractually responsible for supplying inducted workers. The operator carries the practical duty of care and the operational consequence of an untrained person on the floor. Paperwork flows between them; comprehension does not necessarily follow.
What works:
Deliver induction directly rather than accepting agency assurance. A localized module the worker completes on arrival, or before arrival on their own device, is the only reliable control.
Tie floor access to verified completion, in the language the worker selected.
Record language of delivery in the training record. This is both a defensibility measure and the data that shows whether your language set matches your workforce.
Give agencies the material. Agencies supplying multilingual crews will use localized content if it exists and will not create it themselves. Providing it improves what arrives.
Re-induct on return. Seasonal workers returning after months away should refresh, and a short localized refresher is cheap.
Terminology and Signage Alignment
Warehouse vocabulary is concrete and maps to physical things, which makes precision more important than elegance.
Terms requiring locked renderings:
Equipment names by type, matched to what the site actually calls them.
Pedestrian route, crossing, exclusion zone, and traffic control vocabulary.
Racking components and load terminology, including safe working load.
Pre-use check and defect reporting vocabulary.
PPE items as labelled on site.
Emergency terminology, standardised across the network.
Signage and floor marking text, matched exactly to what is physically installed.
Role titles, particularly those with authority — first aider, fire marshal, banksman, supervisor.

The signage alignment point is the one most often missed. Warehouses are dense with visual instruction — floor markings, racking labels, zone signs, hazard notices — and a training video using different vocabulary from the signage leaves the worker unable to connect the two. Terminology should be sourced from the physical site, and where sites differ within a network, that variation needs handling.
Delivery Realities
Personal devices, often modest. Content must work on a wide range of phones.
Connectivity is patchy inside large steel structures. Offline playback with deferred sync is necessary.
Noise is constant. Captions are not optional; provide both localized audio and high-contrast captions.
Time is compressed. Peak-season inductions happen at scale under time pressure. Short modules are the only realistic format.

Pre-arrival delivery is a genuine advantage. Sending induction content to a worker's phone before their first shift removes the bottleneck of inducting everyone on site, and gives the worker time to watch at their own pace in their own language.

That last point is worth emphasising. The main operational objection to thorough induction is that it consumes floor time during the busiest weeks of the year. Localized content delivered ahead of arrival converts that objection into an advantage.
![Warehouse team briefing before a shift
](https://octavia.lunartech.ai)
Fleet and Driver Content
Logistics operators typically have a driver population alongside the warehouse workforce, with different needs.

Content that matters: vehicle checks and defect reporting, load security, drivers' hours and rest rules, delivery site safety and reversing, incident and collision procedure, fuel and telematics systems, and customer-site specific requirements.

Delivery differs too. Drivers consume content in cabs, during breaks, and at depots, on their own phones, frequently with limited connectivity. Audio-first content works particularly well for this population, since much of it can be understood without watching, and short modules fit break structures.
Drivers are also frequently agency or owner-operator rather than employed, which reproduces the verification gap discussed above.
Measuring It
Logistics operations are heavily instrumented, which makes the business case unusually demonstrable.

Metrics worth segmenting by language: incident and near-miss rates, particularly pedestrian-vehicle interactions; manual handling injury rates; equipment damage and racking damage rates; pick accuracy and error rates, since misunderstood instruction produces quality failures as well as safety ones; induction assessment pass rates; time-to-productivity for new starters; and early attrition, which frequently correlates with people who did not understand what they were asked to do.

That last one often surprises operators. Workers who cannot follow the instruction they were given are more likely to leave in the first two weeks, and reducing early attrition in a high-turnover environment has direct and easily calculated value.
A Working Checklist
Start with induction, pedestrian-vehicle segregation, and manual handling.
Build a short-tenure variant for seasonal and agency workers rather than pushing everyone through the full curriculum.
Deliver induction content to workers before arrival where possible.
Verify completion at floor access rather than accepting agency paperwork.
Record language of delivery in training records.
Source terminology from site signage, racking labels, and equipment as actually named on site.
Provide both localized audio and high-contrast captions given ambient noise.
Build offline-capable modules with modest file sizes.
Treat driver content separately, favouring audio-first short modules.
Segment incident, damage, accuracy, and early-attrition data by language.
Peak Season Readiness
The single highest-leverage operational decision in this sector is preparing localized onboarding before the peak hiring wave rather than during it.
A practical sequence:
Finalise content three months out. Induction, segregation, manual handling, and the equipment modules for the truck types in use, in the languages your agency partners actually supply.
Confirm the language set with agencies two months out. They know what the incoming cohort speaks, and the profile shifts year to year with labour market conditions.

Test pre-arrival delivery six weeks out. Sending induction content to a worker's phone before their first shift is the mechanism that removes training from the floor during your busiest weeks, and it needs to be proven before you depend on it.
Brief supervisors two weeks out. They will be the ones interpreting informally when something is unclear, and giving them the terminology and the modules improves what they pass on.
Monitor completion daily during the ramp. A gap between people on the floor and people inducted is visible immediately in the data and invisible on the shop floor until something happens.

Debrief afterwards. Which languages were actually needed, which modules were rewatched, where assessment failures clustered. This is the cheapest available input to next year's programme and it is routinely not collected.
Operators that treat peak readiness as a planned annual cycle rather than an annual emergency find the localization work becomes routine and the cost falls each year.
Frequently Asked Questions
Is it worth localizing training for workers who may only stay six weeks?

Yes, and arguably more than for permanent staff. Short-tenure workers have no accumulated experience to fall back on and no time to acquire it informally, so the training material carries the entire load. They are also disproportionately represented in incident statistics precisely because they are new. A short-tenure module variant keeps the cost proportionate.
How do we handle agency-supplied workers?

Deliver induction directly rather than relying on agency assurance, tie floor access to verified completion in the worker's chosen language, and record that language in the training record. Provide the localized material to agencies as well — they will use it if it exists and will not produce it themselves.
What is the highest-value content to localize first?

Site induction, pedestrian and vehicle segregation, and manual handling technique. Segregation carries the highest consequence, manual handling the highest frequency, and induction reaches everyone. Together they cover the large majority of a new worker's actual exposure.
Where should warehouse terminology come from?

From the physical site — floor markings, racking labels, zone signage, equipment as it is actually named locally, and the wording on hazard notices. Warehouses are dense with visual instruction, and training that uses different vocabulary from the signage leaves workers unable to connect the two. Where sites in a network differ, that variation needs explicit handling.
What business case actually persuades operations leadership?

Early attrition and productivity, usually more than safety statistics. Workers who cannot follow their instructions are more likely to leave within two weeks, and in a high-turnover operation the cost of that is easy to calculate. Pair it with incident rates, equipment and racking damage, and pick accuracy, all segmented by language of training delivery.
Does localized training slow down the onboarding process?

It generally speeds it up, provided the content is delivered before arrival. The bottleneck in peak-season onboarding is trainer availability on the floor, not the worker's time, and content watched on a personal phone before the first shift removes that constraint entirely. Sites that adopt pre-arrival delivery typically report shorter time-to-productive rather than longer.
How many languages does a typical distribution centre need?

Fewer than the number of nationalities present, and more than one. Most operators find three to five languages cover the large majority of their agency-supplied workforce in a given region, with the specific set shifting year to year. Confirm it with your agency partners ahead of each peak rather than carrying last year's assumption forward.

title: Construction Site Safety Video Translation
excerpt: Construction has the most linguistically diverse workforce of any major industry and the least translated safety material.

children.text: ![Construction site with scaffolding and cranes
](https://octavia.lunartech.ai)
The Most Multilingual Workplace There Is

Construction sites in most developed economies are among the most linguistically diverse workplaces that exist. A single project may have crews whose first languages include Polish, Romanian, Portuguese, Spanish, Punjabi, Nepali, Tagalog, Turkish, Arabic, and several more, working alongside each other under a principal contractor who communicates in one.

It is also one of the most hazardous industries, with fatality and serious-injury rates well above the average across the economy, and a hazard profile — falls from height, struck-by, caught-between, electrocution — where a single misunderstanding produces an immediate and irreversible outcome.

The combination should make construction the leading adopter of safety localization. In practice it is among the laggards, for structural reasons: work is delivered through deep subcontracting chains, crews change constantly, projects are temporary, margins are thin, and the party carrying the legal duty often has no direct employment relationship with the person at risk.
None of those obstacles are insurmountable, and the ones that matter most are addressable with content rather than contract restructuring.
Content Worth Localizing
Construction safety communication has a fairly standard shape, and it sorts cleanly by value.

Site induction. Delivered to every person entering the site, covering site-specific hazards, layout, emergency arrangements, muster points, permit requirements, and site rules. Universally required, usually delivered as a rushed group briefing, and very poorly absorbed by anyone following in a second language. This is the highest-value target by a wide margin.

Toolbox talks. Short, frequent, task-specific briefings delivered at the point of work. High volume, repetitive across projects, and ideal for a localized library since the same fifty or so topics recur endlessly.
Method statements and safe systems of work. Task-specific procedure for higher-risk activities. Dense, formal, and frequently written in a register that is difficult even for native speakers.
Plant and equipment operation. Machine-specific instruction, updated as equipment changes.
Emergency procedure. Evacuation, rescue from height, first aid for specific injury types, incident reporting. Needed under stress, when second-language comprehension is weakest.
Permit-to-work briefings. Hot works, confined space, excavation, isolation. The permit system depends entirely on everyone understanding the same boundaries.
The practical starting point is site induction plus the twenty most-used toolbox talks. That combination covers the majority of the workforce's exposure and is genuinely reusable across projects.
The Subcontractor Chain Problem
The structural difficulty in construction is that the principal contractor sets the safety requirements but the person doing the hazardous work may be three or four contractual layers away.

Each layer is supposed to pass down the requirements and confirm competence. In practice, information degrades at every transfer, and the crew at the bottom may receive a briefing delivered by a supervisor who is themselves working in a second language, summarising a document nobody in the crew can read.
What works:
Provide the content directly to workers rather than relying on the chain. A localized induction a worker completes on their own phone bypasses the degradation entirely.

Verify at the gate, not on paper. Site access control tied to confirmed induction completion — in a language the worker selected — is the control that actually closes the loop. Trusting a subcontractor's paperwork does not.

Record the language of delivery. In an investigation, the question is whether that individual received comprehensible instruction. A record showing induction completed in Romanian is evidence; a record showing induction completed is not.

Make it easy for subcontractors to use. Small subcontractors will not build their own localized material. Giving them ready-made content in the languages their crews speak is more effective than requiring them to produce it.
Cover the supervisor layer explicitly. Supervisors frequently interpret informally for their crews. Giving them the terminology and the localized material improves what they pass on.
![Workers reviewing plans on a construction site
](https://octavia.lunartech.ai)
Terminology That Maps to Physical Things
Construction safety vocabulary refers to physical objects, physical actions, and physical boundaries. A near-synonym is not good enough, because the worker has to connect the word to the thing.
Terms requiring locked renderings per language:
Fall protection: harness, lanyard, anchor point, guardrail, toe board, edge protection, fall arrest, work restraint.
Access equipment: scaffold, tower, podium, mobile elevating work platform, ladder classifications.
Excavation: shoring, battering, trench box, spoil, services, permit.
Lifting: sling, shackle, exclusion zone, banksman or signaller, safe working load.
Electrical: isolation, lock off, permit, live, dead, proving.
Confined space: entry permit, atmospheric testing, rescue plan, top man.
PPE items, matched to what is written on the equipment and on site signage.
Permit types and the authority roles attached to them.
Signage text, matched exactly to the physical signs on site.
Emergency vocabulary, standardised and pre-agreed.

The alignment requirement matters more than translation elegance. If the sign on the hoarding says one thing and the induction video says another, the worker cannot connect them. Terminology must be sourced from what is physically present on site and from the regulator's published vocabulary, not generated independently by a training function.
Preserving the Force of Instruction
Safety instruction is deliberately absolute — never, always, must, before any, under no circumstances — because the situations it governs do not admit judgement.

Fluent translation drifts toward natural register, and natural register hedges. An instruction that becomes "you should normally" where the source said "you must always" has converted a rule into a suggestion.
Controls:
Lock imperative and absolute constructions as terminology with approved renderings.
Substitute legally required warnings from approved local documentation rather than translating them.
Review against source by someone with both language competence and site competence. A translator without construction knowledge will not notice that a rule became advice.
Verify sequence language explicitly — before, after, only once, not until — since procedure depends on order.
Run a numeric check across every height, load, distance, voltage, and time value.
Delivery on Site
Construction sites impose delivery constraints that office training does not.
Connectivity is often poor. Basements, steel structures, and remote sites frequently have no usable signal. Content must download and play offline, with completion syncing later.
Devices are personal and varied. Workers use their own phones across a wide range of capability. Large files exclude people.
Conditions are bright and loud. Screens are hard to read in sun; audio is hard to hear near plant. Provide both localized audio and high-contrast captions rather than choosing one.
Time is fragmented. Content is watched in a van before shift, at a break, or at the gate. Short single-topic modules work; hour-long courses do not.
Gloves and PPE limit interaction. Interfaces needing precise touch input fail in the field.
These constraints point to the same answer as the content analysis: short, single-topic, offline-capable modules with both audio and captions.
![Site supervisor briefing a crew
](https://octavia.lunartech.ai)
Choosing Languages
Base language selection on the actual workforce, not on assumptions.

Useful sources: site access records, which frequently capture nationality; subcontractor workforce declarations; interpreter and translation requests; incident reports where language was a factor; and — most directly — asking supervisors which languages their crews actually use.

Two cautions. First, nationality is not language: a Romanian passport holder may be a Hungarian speaker, and a Spanish-speaking crew may include Quechua or Mixtec speakers whose Spanish is itself a second language. Second, workforce composition changes rapidly between projects and phases, so a language set fixed at project start will drift.

A practical approach is to establish a core set of four to six languages covering the bulk of the regional workforce, refresh it each project, and add on demand where a subcontractor brings a crew speaking something outside the set.
Making the Case
Safety spend competes for budget, and the argument lands better with operational data than with principle.

Arguments that carry weight: incident and near-miss rates segmented by language group, where the data exists; induction assessment pass rates by language, where a gap is easy to demonstrate; rework and defect rates, since misunderstood instruction produces poor work as well as unsafe work; insurance and client prequalification requirements, which increasingly ask about workforce competence assurance; and regulatory exposure, since most safety regimes require instruction in a form the worker can understand, and attendance records do not demonstrate that.

That last point is the strongest one. A contractor relying on training delivered in a language a worker does not follow may not be discharging its duty, regardless of how complete the signature sheet looks.
A Working Checklist
Start with site induction plus the twenty most-used toolbox talks.
Source terminology from site signage, equipment labelling, permit paperwork, and the regulator's published vocabulary.
Lock imperative and absolute constructions so instructions do not soften.
Have output reviewed by someone with both language and site competence.
Provide content directly to workers rather than relying on the subcontract chain.
Verify induction completion at site access control, not on subcontractor paperwork.
Record the language of delivery in competence records.
Build modules short, offline-capable, and modest in file size.
Supply both localized audio and high-contrast captions.
Refresh the language set each project against actual workforce composition.
Sustaining the Programme
Safety localization programmes frequently launch well and decay, because the initial build is project-funded and the maintenance is not.
What keeps them alive:
Attach ownership to a role, not an individual. Programmes that depend on one enthusiastic health and safety manager end when that person moves on, which in construction is frequently.
Refresh the language set every project. Workforce composition changes between projects and phases, and a language set fixed at programme launch drifts out of alignment within a year.
Treat induction as the permanent core. It is delivered to everyone, it changes rarely, and it carries the majority of the value. Toolbox talks accumulate around it over time.

Feed every incident and near-miss finding back into terminology. A misunderstanding identified once should be corrected everywhere, and an investigation process that does not update the glossary wastes its most useful output.
Budget it as a line item. Safety training localization funded from a project contingency disappears when the contingency does. A standing budget line survives leadership changes.
Report usage by language annually. Completion rates and language distribution shared with leadership keep the programme visible and make its continuation a default rather than an argument.

Contractors that sustain this find the ongoing cost is far below the initial build, provided the scope stayed focused on induction and the recurring toolbox talk library rather than expanding to cover every method statement.
Frequently Asked Questions
Who is responsible for translating safety material in a subcontracting chain?

The duty to ensure workers receive comprehensible instruction generally rests with whoever controls the site, regardless of employment relationship, and it cannot be fully delegated down the chain. Practically, the principal contractor providing localized content directly — and verifying completion at site access rather than accepting subcontractor paperwork — is both the more effective control and the more defensible position.
What is the biggest translation risk in construction safety content?

Softening of absolutes. Safety instruction is deliberately rigid, and fluent translation drifts toward natural register, which hedges. "Must always" becoming "should normally" converts a rule into a suggestion, and the resulting sentence reads perfectly well, so it survives review by anyone without site knowledge.
Where should safety terminology come from?

From what is physically present: site signage, equipment labelling, permit documentation, and the regulator's published vocabulary in that language. Terminology developed independently by a training function will not match what the worker sees on the hoarding or the harness, and a term that does not match the label is worse than no term at all.
How do we decide which languages to support?

From site access records, subcontractor workforce declarations, interpreter requests, and directly asking supervisors what their crews speak. Do not infer language from nationality — passport country and first language frequently differ, and some crews speak a regional language for which the national language is itself a second language. Refresh the set each project.
What format works for site delivery?

Short single-topic modules, downloadable for offline playback, small file size, with both localized audio and high-contrast captions, playable on a personal phone in bright sun and high noise. Connectivity is unreliable on most sites, viewing happens in fragments, and long courses requiring sustained attention and a data connection do not survive contact with site conditions.

title: Translate Video to Nepali: Honorifics, Devanagari, and Diaspora Reach
excerpt: Nepali makes you choose how much respect to show before you can finish a sentence. English gives the system nothing to go on.

children.text: ![Himalayan mountain range at sunrise
](https://octavia.lunartech.ai)
A Distributed Audience

Nepali has around thirty-two million speakers. Roughly half live in Nepal; the rest are distributed across India — particularly Sikkim, West Bengal, and Assam — Bhutan, and a large and economically significant migrant workforce across the Gulf states, Malaysia, South Korea, Japan, and increasingly Europe, Australia, and North America.

That distribution shapes the localization case in a specific way. A very large share of the Nepali-speaking audience for practical, informational video consists of migrant workers: people who need employment rights information, remittance guidance, health and safety instruction, immigration procedure, and connection to home. This audience is mobile-first, data-constrained, and frequently underserved by any content in their own language.
The commercial audience in Nepal itself is growing quickly with mobile internet penetration, and the diaspora audience has disposable income and strong demand for Nepali-language media.
For organisations in employment, financial services, health, government, and development, Nepali is often a higher-value localization target than its speaker count alone suggests.
Honorifics Are the Central Grammatical Problem
Nepali encodes social relationship into its grammar in a way that English does not, and this is the single biggest source of translation error.

Nepali has multiple levels of second-person address and correspondingly different verb forms, conventionally described as three or four grades running from a low-respect form used with children, close intimates, and in certain traditional contexts, through a mid-grade used among peers, to high-respect forms used with elders, strangers, and superiors, and a very high honorific used for the most formal or reverential contexts.

Choosing the wrong level is not a subtle stylistic slip. Addressing an adult stranger with the low-grade form is genuinely rude. Addressing a peer with the highest honorific is stiff to the point of sounding sarcastic.
English's single "you" gives a translation system no information at all about which to use. Left unspecified, it will pick a default, and that default will be wrong for a meaningful share of content.
Practical guidance:
Specify the level before translation. State who is speaking and to whom, and what relationship the content assumes.

For general audience content, the high-respect grade is the safe default. Public communication, instructional content, customer-facing material, and anything addressing an unknown adult audience should use it.
Mid-grade suits peer-to-peer creator content where the presenter is positioning themselves as a friend rather than an authority.
Reserve the highest honorific for genuinely formal, ceremonial, or reverential contexts. Overusing it makes ordinary content sound archaic.
Never mix grades within a single video addressed to one audience. This is the most visible failure and reads as careless.
Honorifics also affect third-person reference and certain nouns, so the choice propagates further than pronouns alone.
Devanagari and the Hindi Problem

Nepali is written in Devanagari, the same script as Hindi and Marathi. This creates the same category of risk described elsewhere: content misconfigured to Hindi produces Devanagari output that looks entirely plausible to anyone who does not read the language.

Nepali and Hindi share script and a substantial amount of Sanskrit-derived vocabulary, and they are not the same language. Grammar differs, everyday vocabulary differs, and the honorific system differs. Nepali speakers notice substitution immediately.
Technical points:
Set language codes explicitly to ne in subtitle files, metadata, and platform fields. Generic Devanagari or Hindi tagging affects discoverability and downstream language handling.
Have a Nepali reader verify the first output from any new pipeline.
Font support is generally good since Devanagari is widely covered, which removes one common class of problem.
Line height must accommodate the horizontal head line plus vowel marks above and conjunct forms below the baseline.
Text expansion runs roughly fifteen to twenty percent longer than English.
Numerals are conventionally Western digits in contemporary Nepali media, though Devanagari numerals appear in some official and traditional contexts.

Dates deserve specific attention: Nepal officially uses the Bikram Sambat calendar, which is roughly fifty-seven years ahead of the Gregorian and has different month boundaries. Content referencing dates for a Nepal audience should handle this deliberately rather than converting mechanically, and diaspora audiences may expect Gregorian.
![Recording microphone in a small studio
](https://octavia.lunartech.ai)
Register and Vocabulary
Nepali has a formal register with heavy Sanskrit-derived vocabulary and a more accessible everyday register.
Standard Nepali, based on the Kathmandu valley variety, is the form used in education, broadcasting, and formal contexts.
Regional varieties across Nepal differ in vocabulary and pronunciation, and Nepali as spoken in India carries additional influences.

Formal Sanskritised register is used in government and legal communication and can be dense. Public communication increasingly favours plainer language, and localization should generally follow that trend rather than reaching for the most formal available vocabulary.
Terminology positions:
Technical and product vocabulary is generally borrowed from English in everyday speech. Sanskrit-derived coinages for modern technical concepts are frequently not recognised.
Government, legal, and administrative terminology has established Nepali forms that should be used, particularly for anything referencing official processes or documents.
Institutional and document names should be retained in their official form so the audience can match them to real paperwork, with a plain Nepali explanation alongside.
Avoid Hindi vocabulary substitution, which is the specific failure Nepali speakers react to.
Lock these as custom terminology before translation.
Timing and Dubbing

Nepali follows subject-object-verb order, so the verb resolves at the end of the clause. As with other SOV languages, narration timed to an on-screen event may need restructuring so meaning lands where the picture expects it.
Practical guidance:
Allow narration to run longer than the English source rather than compressing it.
Verify clause-final verbs and honorific verb endings survive segment boundaries intact — truncating an honorific ending changes the register.
Check alignment where narration references visible elements.
Confirm speaker separation before generating audio for multi-speaker content.
Have a native speaker verify the honorific level is consistent throughout the generated audio, which is easy to lose track of across a long piece.
Reaching the Migrant Workforce Audience
This audience deserves specific consideration because it is large, high-need, and structurally underserved.
Characteristics that shape delivery:
Mobile-only, on metered data. Keep file sizes modest, provide downloadable versions, and avoid designs requiring sustained high bandwidth.
Audio matters more than text. Literacy varies, and viewers are frequently watching in short breaks or in noisy environments. Dubbed audio reaches more people than subtitles alone.
Messaging platforms carry distribution. Content designed to be shared within messaging groups reaches this audience far more effectively than content requiring a website visit.
Short modules work better than long courses. Viewing happens in fragments — a break, a commute, before sleep.

Trust routes through community. Content shared by a community organisation, a recruitment intermediary that workers trust, or a diaspora media outlet is acted on; the same content from an unfamiliar official source frequently is not.
Practical, concrete instruction outperforms explanation. What to do, where to go, what document to bring, who to call.

Content types with the clearest value: employment rights and contract terms, remittance procedures and fees, health and safety instruction, healthcare access in the destination country, immigration and visa procedure, and returnee reintegration information.
![Person watching a video on a phone during a break
](https://octavia.lunartech.ai)
Subtitles or Dubbing
Dub when reaching the migrant workforce audience, when content is instructional, when literacy in the audience varies, or when viewers are watching on small screens in fragmented conditions.
Subtitle when the audience is urban and educated, when preserving the original speaker matters, or when content is short-form social video.
Both where possible. Nepali audiences on streaming platforms commonly use subtitles alongside audio.
For public-interest and development content specifically, dubbed audio plus an audio-only version for radio and messaging distribution is the combination that maximises reach per unit of effort.
A Working Checklist
Confirm the target is Nepali, not Hindi, and set language codes to ne explicitly.
Have a Nepali reader verify the first output from any new pipeline.
Specify the honorific level before translation, stating the speaker-audience relationship.
Default to the high-respect grade for general audience and public-facing content.
Never mix honorific grades within one asset.
Lock official document and institution names in their real form with plain Nepali explanation.
Handle Bikram Sambat versus Gregorian dates deliberately for the intended audience.
Increase subtitle line height for Devanagari marks above and below the baseline.
Prioritise dubbed audio for migrant-workforce and public-interest content.
Produce an audio-only version for radio and messaging distribution.
Planning a First Project
A first localization project into Nepali goes more smoothly with a few decisions made deliberately rather than discovered mid-way.

Pick content that suits the language, not just the market. Evergreen explanatory content with clean single-speaker audio is the right starting point. Content dense with overlapping speech, heavy idiom, or tight narration-to-visual sync will expose every weakness in the workflow at once and teach you less.

Budget review time honestly. Expect the first assets in a new language to need substantially more review than the tenth, because the recurring corrections have not yet become locked terminology. Pricing or scheduling on first-job effort will overstate your steady-state cost considerably.

Recruit the reviewer before you need them. A native speaker who knows the subject matter is worth considerably more than a general translator, and finding one under deadline pressure produces a worse choice than finding one in advance.

Run a short sample end to end first. Two minutes of representative content through the full pipeline — transcript, terminology, translation, generation, delivery — surfaces rendering, timing, and register problems while they are cheap to fix.
Keep the reviewed transcript. It is the input to every future language and every future subtitle track, and regenerating it each time discards correction work already paid for.
Fix the honorific level before translation starts. It affects verb forms throughout, it cannot be corrected by find-and-replace afterwards, and English provides no cue for which grade applies.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is the biggest source of error in Nepali translation?

Honorific level. Nepali has multiple grades of second-person address with corresponding verb forms, and choosing wrongly is genuinely rude or absurdly stiff rather than merely imprecise. English's single "you" gives the system no information, so the level must be specified before translation along with the assumed speaker-audience relationship. For general audience content, the high-respect grade is the safe default.
Is Nepali similar enough to Hindi to reuse Hindi content?

No. They share Devanagari script and Sanskrit-derived vocabulary but differ in grammar, everyday vocabulary, and the honorific system. The shared script means misconfigured Hindi output looks entirely plausible to anyone who does not read the language, which is exactly why a Nepali reader should verify the first output from any new pipeline and language codes should be set explicitly.
How should dates be handled for a Nepali audience?

Deliberately. Nepal officially uses the Bikram Sambat calendar, roughly fifty-seven years ahead of the Gregorian with different month boundaries. Content aimed at audiences in Nepal should use it where dates matter, while diaspora audiences frequently expect Gregorian. Mechanical conversion without deciding which convention applies produces confusing results.
Should I dub or subtitle Nepali content?

Dub for the migrant workforce audience, instructional content, and anywhere literacy varies — this is where most of the practical demand sits, and audio reaches substantially more people. Subtitle for urban educated audiences, short-form social video, or where preserving the original speaker matters. For public-interest content, dubbed audio plus an audio-only version for radio and messaging distribution maximises reach.
What content is most valuable to localize into Nepali?

Practical information for the migrant workforce: employment rights and contract terms, remittance procedures and fees, occupational health and safety, healthcare access in destination countries, visa and immigration procedure, and reintegration guidance. This audience is large, high-need, and served by almost nobody in its own language.
Related reading:

Translate Video to Marathi
